name: Salt water rinse

lead: A salt water rinse is a homemade mouthwash of warm water with dissolved salt. People use it to soothe sore gums and keep the mouth clean, for healthier gums and a fresher mouth at almost no cost.

Wikipedia describes saline as a mechanical cleanser with antiseptic action, because the solution is hypertonic to bacteria. A school-based randomised trial compared salt water with chlorhexidine for effects on dental plaque and oral microbes.

paras: People mix salt into warm water at home and swish it gently, often after meals or brushing, or when gums feel sore. It is commonly used alongside regular brushing and flossing.
Low risk. After dental extractions, guidance advises holding the rinse gently at first rather than swishing vigorously.

angle.text: Warm salt water rinses are a low-cost home habit for soothing sore gums and keeping the mouth clean, supporting healthier gums and a fresher mouth. Saline is described as a mechanical cleanser with antiseptic action, and one school trial compared it with chlorhexidine.

lead: A salt water rinse is a rinse of warm water with dissolved salt, used as a low-cost mouthwash for gum soreness and mouth hygiene. Wikipedia describes saline as a mechanical cleanser with antiseptic action because it is hypertonic to bacteria.[1]

A school-based randomised trial compared salt water with chlorhexidine for effects on dental plaque and oral microbes.[2] Wikipedia's mouthwash article does not discuss salt water for gingivitis specifically or for bad breath.[1]

paras: Salt water gargles appear in early accounts, including ancient Chinese records from about 94 BCE and Hippocratic recommendations, though dating is imprecise.[1]

A randomised controlled trial in schoolchildren compared salt water rinse with chlorhexidine mouthwash against plaque and oral microbial counts, after first measuring the minimum inhibitory concentration of salt water against four oral bacteria.[2] Wikipedia notes saline guidance in oral mucositis from cancer therapy, where it is reported as about as effective as other rinses for pain and healing time.[1]

After tooth extraction, dental guidance cited by Wikipedia is to begin warm salt water mouth baths about 24 hours later, holding the liquid passively at first so the blood clot is not dislodged.[1] Salt water is also noted as an option for people sensitive to mouthwash ingredients.[1]
Salt rinses are mentioned in lifestyle discussions as a cheap gum soother.

lore.intro: Salt water rinse is discussed as an inexpensive home remedy.
